name: Manganese tripeptide-1

lead: Manganese tripeptide-1 is a cosmetic peptide complex used in facial serums for photodamaged skin. It is described as the manganese counterpart of the copper peptide GHK. People use it to address sun damage and dark spots and to even out skin tone.

A single 12-week facial study, in which participants used a serum with the complex twice daily, reported improvement in photodamage signs, especially hyperpigmentation, as judged by participants and a blinded investigator. The study does not establish a mechanism; the ingredient is presented as an analogue of GHK-type peptides. Independent controlled trials have not been identified.

paras: It is applied as a facial serum, twice daily in the published study, with changes judged over about 12 weeks. People typically use it alongside sunscreen as part of a routine for pigmentation and photodamage.
The one study reported good tolerability with no significant inflammation. Long-term and comparative safety data have not been published in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Manganese tripeptide-1 is a manganese analogue of GHK used in facial serums for sun damage and dark spots, aiming for clearer, more even skin tone. It targets photodamage and uneven pigmentation. A single 12-week facial study reported improved photodamage signs, most notably pigmentation.

lead: Manganese tripeptide-1 is a cosmetic ingredient made of a manganese complex of a tripeptide, described as the manganese counterpart of the copper-binding peptide GHK. It is used in facial serums that aim to even out sun-related uneven pigmentation and improve the look of photodamaged skin.[1][2]

The published human evidence is a single study in which participants used a serum containing the complex twice daily for up to 12 weeks. The participants and a blinded investigator noted improvement in several signs of photodamage, most notably those related to hyperpigmentation, and the serum was reported to be well tolerated.[1] Independent controlled trials have not been identified.

The copper form, GHK-Cu, was first isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973 and is marketed as copper tripeptide-1; Wikipedia describes its facial anti-aging evidence as coming mostly from cell and animal work plus small, short facial studies.[2]

paras: The ingredient appears in topical serums aimed at signs of facial photoaging such as discoloration and rough texture.[1]

One published study evaluated a facial serum containing manganese tripeptide-1 applied twice a day for up to 12 weeks. Participants and a blinded investigator noted improvement in several photodamage parameters, predominantly those linked to hyperpigmentation, with overall photodamage ranking moving from moderate to mild on average. The authors reported no significant skin inflammation attributable to the complex.[1] The report describes a serum formulation rather than the isolated ingredient, and no comparison against other treatments is described in the abstract.

GHK-Cu was first isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973 and is marketed as copper tripeptide-1.[2] Evidence for GHK-Cu in facial anti-aging is described in Wikipedia as coming mostly from cell and animal work plus small, short facial studies.[2]
Manganese tripeptide-1 is a less common relative of copper peptides in the cosmetic ingredient market. No looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.

timeline.event: GHK-Cu, the copper form of the related tripeptide, is first isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart.[2]
A facial study of a manganese tripeptide-1 serum for photodamage is published in the Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy.[1]
